# 4xx

*Status code* · also written 4xx errors · client errors

The class of HTTP status codes for client errors; apart from 429 they do not slow Google's crawling.

**Glossary** (*HTTP status code classes*): 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error. Each class affects crawling differently, and 429 is the 4xx code that tells Google to slow down instead of saying there is nothing at the URL.

8 claims mention it: 1 from Google's documentation, 4 shown or said at the event (1 confirmed by Google docs, 3 consistent with Google docs), 3 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes).

- [`D1-C072`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Docs: 4xx status codes other than 429 have no effect on crawl rate. `[D1-C072, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D1-C353`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: 429 Too Many Requests is the exception among 4xx codes: instead of meaning there is nothing at the URL, it tells Google's crawler to slow down, and Google slows its crawling. `[D1-C353, stage, Cherry Prommawin, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C345`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: HTTP status codes fall into five classes, 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and each class affects crawling differently. `[D1-C345, stage, Cherry Prommawin, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C365`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features. `[D1-C365, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C385`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: 4xx responses do not affect a site's crawl budget, because Google expects pages, content and products to come and go as a natural part of the web. `[D1-C385, stage, Google, Day 1]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C386`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092). `[D1-C386, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C419`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'. `[D1-C419, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C913`](../sessions/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) Analysis: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page. `[D2-C913, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`

## For developers

- `DEV-ERR-01` **MUST** · Documented: Return 404 or 410 for removed and non-existent URLs (2 of its claims mention it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-SRV-09` **AVOID** · Documented: Do not answer crawlers with 401, 402 or 403 on pages that should be in Search (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
